name: Thessaloniki
info: Thessaloniki is a city on the Thermaic Gulf in northern Greece, founded around 315 BCE by Cassander of Macedon, later the second city of the Byzantine Empire, a large Ottoman port and the second-largest city of Greece.

facts.founded: Around 315 BCE by King Cassander of Macedon, on or near the site of the ancient town of Therma and 26 other local villages; he named it after his wife Thessalonike, a half-sister of Alexander the Great.
facts.where: On the northern edge of the Thermaic Gulf, at the north-west corner of the Aegean Sea, bounded on the west by the delta of the Axios, in Central Macedonia, Greece.
facts.known: A city on the Roman Via Egnatia; Galerius's palace, arch and mausoleum; St Demetrius; the second city of the Byzantine Empire; the home of Cyril and Methodius; the Zealots of 1342; the largest Sephardic Jewish community; the Young Turk Revolution of 1908; the Great Fire of 1917
facts.today: Thessaloniki is the second-largest city of Greece and the capital of the region of Central Macedonia.

t: Cassander founded the city around 315 BCE, the Romans made it a provincial capital on the Via Egnatia, and under Galerius and later emperors it became the second city of the Byzantine world after Constantinople.
The Ottomans took it in 1430, and after 1492 Sephardic Jews from Spain settled there, so that by 1519 they made up 54% of the city's population.
Greece took the city in 1912, the fire of 1917 destroyed its centre, the exchange of populations changed its makeup, and the deportation of 1943 destroyed its Jewish community.
dyk: In 1519, according to Ottoman archives, Thessaloniki had 15,715 Jews, 6,870 Muslims and about 6,635 Christians, and the Jews were 54% of the city's population.
ev: Cassander founds the city and names it after his wife Thessalonike
St Demetrius becomes the patron saint of the city
A naval force led by Leo of Tripoli sacks the city
Sultan Murad II captures the city from the Venetians
Ottoman archives record a Jewish majority of 54%
The Ottoman garrison surrenders to the Greek army
A fire destroys most of the old centre and leaves 72,000 people homeless
The deportation of the city's Jews to Auschwitz begins

sections.origins:
Thessaloniki lies on the northern edge of the Thermaic Gulf, at the north-west corner of the Aegean Sea, and the delta of the Axios bounds it on the west. The city was founded around 315 BCE by King Cassander of Macedon, on or near the site of the ancient town of Therma and 26 other local villages. He named it after his wife Thessalonike, a half-sister of Alexander the Great and a princess of Macedonia as daughter of Philip II. Her name means "Thessalian victory" and honours a Macedonian victory at the Battle of Crocus Field in 353 or 352 BCE. A popular Greek legend holds that Thessalonike became a mermaid who lived in the Aegean after Alexander's death.

The city was built 40 km south-east of Pella, the capital of the Kingdom of Macedonia, and Pella remained the capital until the kingdom fell. Under the kingdom Thessaloniki kept its own autonomy and a parliament of its own, and it became the most important city in Macedonia. It had its first walls, enclosing and protecting the city, as early as the 2nd century BCE. The name Saloniki is first attested in Greek in the Chronicle of the Morea in the 14th century, and the geographer al-Idrisi already called the city Salunik in the 12th century.
sections.growth:
Under the Romans Thessaloniki grew into an important trade hub on the Via Egnatia, the road that linked Dyrrhachium with Byzantium and carried trade between Europe and Asia. The Romans built a spacious harbour there, the Burrowed Harbour, which served the city's trade until the 18th century, and silt from the Axios later allowed land to be reclaimed and the port to be extended. The city also lay at the southern end of the main north to south route through the Balkans, along the valleys of the Morava and the Axios. Under the tetrarchy Galerius had an imperial palace, a new hippodrome, a triumphal arch and a mausoleum built there.

From the first years of the Byzantine Empire Thessaloniki was counted as its second city after Constantinople, in wealth and in size, with a population of 150,000 in the mid-12th century. In the 14th century its population is put at 100,000 to 150,000, which made it larger than London at that time. Under the Komnenoi its economy expanded, and the city housed an imperial mint and held the fair of St Demetrius each October outside its walls. In 1519 it was both the largest Jewish city in the world and the only one with a Jewish majority. After 1870 the population rose by 70%, and the railway reached the city in 1888.
sections.rulers:
After the Kingdom of Macedonia fell, Thessaloniki passed to Rome. In 128 BCE it became the capital of the Roman province of Macedonia, and in 41 BCE Mark Antony made it a free city. Under the tetrarchy it was the administrative capital of one of the four portions of the empire, held by Galerius. In 379, when the Prefecture of Illyricum was divided between the eastern and western empires, it became the capital of the new prefecture, and by the fall of Rome in 476 it was the second-largest city of the Eastern Roman Empire.

The Fourth Crusade took Constantinople in 1204, and Thessaloniki became the seat of the Kingdom of Thessalonica, the largest vassal of the Latin Empire. In 1224 Theodore Komnenos Doukas of Epirus overran it and made it the capital of the Empire of Thessalonica, and after his defeat at Klokotnitsa in 1230 the city became a vassal of the Second Bulgarian Empire until the Empire of Nicaea took it in 1246. The Ottomans took it after a siege of 1383 to 1387, and the Byzantines recovered it in 1403. Despot Andronikos Palaiologos ceded it to Venice in 1423, and Sultan Murad II captured it on 29 March 1430.

The Ottomans held it for nearly five centuries as the capital of the Sanjak of Selanik, later of the Selanik Eyalet and Vilayet. It passed to the Kingdom of Greece in November 1912, and the Treaty of Bucharest of 1913 confirmed this.
sections.life:
Thessaloniki was among the early centres of Christianity. About 50 CE Paul the Apostle visited the city's chief synagogue on three Sabbaths, and he later wrote two letters to the new church there, which appear in the New Testament as First and Second Thessalonians. In 306 the city acquired a patron saint, St Demetrius, and a basilica in his name was first built in the fifth century. The brothers Cyril and Methodius were natives of the city, and in the ninth century they created the first literary language of the Slavs, Old Church Slavonic, most likely from the Slavic dialect of the hinterland of their home town.

Under the Ottomans the Muslim population grew substantially. The 1478 census recorded 6,094 Christian Orthodox households and 4,320 Muslim ones, and no Jews, but soon after 1500 Sephardic Jews arrived, following their expulsion from Spain under the Alhambra Decree of 1492. Some historians consider that the Ottoman invitation to Jewish settlement was meant to prevent the Christians from dominating the city. Most of the city's tradespeople were Jewish, and the Jewish community spoke Judeo-Spanish, a dialect of Spanish. In 1890 the population was 118,000, of whom 47% were Jews, 22% Turks, 14% Greeks and 8% Bulgarians; in 1913 it was 157,889, with Jews at 39%, Turks 29% and Greeks 25%. The walls were torn down between 1869 and 1889, the first tram ran in 1888, and electric street lighting came in 1908.
sections.crises:
In 390 the city rose in revolt against the detention of a favourite charioteer, and troops under Theodosius I carried out a massacre of its inhabitants. Avars and Slavs besieged the city several times in the sixth and seventh centuries without taking it, as the Miracles of Saint Demetrius narrate. A naval force led by Leo of Tripoli sacked it in 904, and Normans from the Kingdom of Sicily sacked it again in 1185. When Murad II took it in 1430, contemporary reports estimated that about one fifth of the population was enslaved. In May 1821, at the start of the Greek War of Independence, the governor Yusuf Bey had half of more than 400 hostages killed in front of him.

The Great Fire began on 18 August 1917 from an unattended kitchen fire and burned for 32 hours. It destroyed most of the old centre, two churches and many synagogues and mosques, and left 72,000 people homeless, 50,000 of them Jewish according to the Pallis Report, of a population of about 271,157. The government forbade quick rebuilding so that a new plan, headed by the French architect Ernest Hebrard, could be carried out.

Germany occupied the city in April 1941. The Jews were forced into a ghetto, and from 15 March 1943 about 45,000 were deported to Auschwitz and Bergen-Belsen; most were murdered at once, and only 4% of those sent to Auschwitz survived. The earthquakes of June 1978 damaged buildings and monuments, and an apartment building collapsed.
sections.legacy:
Several early Christian and Byzantine monuments of Thessaloniki were added to the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1988, and Byzantine mosaics survive in some of its churches, including the Hagia Sophia and the church of St George. The Arch and Tomb of Galerius also remain. Of the more than 40 minarets of the Ottoman city, most were demolished after 1912 or fell in the fire of 1917, and the only one that survives stands at the Rotonda, which is part of the Arch and Tomb of Galerius. The White Tower, left standing when the old walls were taken down, is the city's main landmark. The Ano Poli, the upper town, escaped the fire of 1917 and keeps its Ottoman and Greek houses, its Byzantine fort the Heptapyrgion and part of the walls.

The plan drawn up after 1917 gave the centre its wide diagonal avenues and monumental squares. The city is also called the Symprotevousa, the "co-capital", after its place beside Constantinople in the Byzantine Empire, and in 1916 it was the seat of the Provisional Government of National Defence under Venizelos. Atatürk was born there in 1881, and the Young Turks began their revolution of 1908 from the city. The Greek exchange of populations after 1922 brought over 160,000 Greek refugees, and the Jewish population fell to a minority for the first time since the 16th century.

The municipality had 319,045 inhabitants in 2021, and the metropolitan area about one million.

summary: Thessaloniki, on the Thermaic Gulf, was founded around 315 BCE by Cassander and became a Roman provincial capital and the second city of the Byzantine Empire. Ottoman rule from 1430 made it a largely Jewish city; Greece took it in 1912, and today it is the second-largest city of Greece.
references: Devin E. Naar, Jewish Salonica: Between the Ottoman Empire and Modern Greece (Stanford University Press, 2016)
Nevra Necipoğlu, Byzantium between the Ottomans and the Latins: Politics and Society in the Late Empire (Cambridge University Press, 2009)
Apostolos E. Vacalopoulos, History of Macedonia 1354–1833 (Institute for Balkan Studies, 1973)
notes: START: founded 'around 315 BC' in both articles, so start -315 with circa true.
GERMAN OCCUPATION: the main article says 8 April 1941, the history article 22 April 1941; I wrote 'April 1941' only.
SURRENDER OF 1912: main article gives 8 November 1912 (26 October Old Style); the history article gives 9 November [27 October O.S.]. I wrote 'November 1912' in the text and labelled the event 1912.
ZEALOTS: 1342 to 1349 (history) versus overthrown 1350 (main); left out of the sections and takeaways.

POPULATION 1917: the history article says the population reached 135,000 in 1917 (and 130,000 at the start of the 20th century), the main article gives about 271,157 at the time of the fire; I used only 271,157 with the fire, and left the 135,000 and 130,000 out.
JEWISH SURVIVORS 1943: main article says 4% of the 45,000 deported to Auschwitz survived; history article says barely a thousand Jews survived. I used the main article's figures only.
1978 EARTHQUAKE: death toll 51 (main) versus forty crushed in one building (history); death toll and magnitude left out.

ROMAN CAPITAL: main article 128 BC for the provincial capital; history article says it was capital of all the Greek provinces for a short time in the 1st century BC and became a Roman city after 168 BC. Used 128 BCE and 41 BCE (free city) from the main article.

OTTOMAN CAPTURES: the history article says the Ottomans took it in 1387 and lost it after 1402; the main article says it surrendered after a siege of 1383 to 1387, submitted again about 1391 and was returned in 1403 under the Treaty of Gallipoli. I used the main article's 1383-1387 siege and the return in 1403. The main article also says the Ottoman siege ran 1422 to 1430 (Ano Poli passage) and that Andronikos ceded it in 1423; both used only loosely.

ST DEMETRIUS: history article says he was Proconsul killed in a Roman prison; main article says Galerius is said to have put him to death and that most scholars hold he was not a native; only the 306 acquisition of the patron saint and the fifth-century basilica are stated.
